meta.title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

exploratory.title: H1 robustness: excluding attention-check failures
exploratory.rationale: Respondents who fail both knowledge questions may not have engaged with the task, so excluding them tests whether registered H1 effects are driven by inattentive respondents.
exploratory.method: Re-fit the registered H1 model (total_score ~ arm × covariates, IPW, HC2) on the subsample with pk_score >= 1 (n=1417 vs 2030 full); compare arm-level ATEs and SEs side by side.
exploratory.finding: Excluding 613 attention-check failures (n 2030→1417) eliminated the two nominally significant registered effects (Automated Flagging p=0.004→ns; AI Literacy Guide p=0.043→ns), suggesting those effects were concentrated among respondents who also passed the knowledge checks.

exploratory.title: H1 heterogeneity by prior AI familiarity
exploratory.rationale: Interventions that teach AI detection may work differently for respondents who already know AI tools versus those who do not; this checks whether registered H1 effects are concentrated among low-familiarity respondents.
exploratory.method: Split sample at the median of ai_scale (0.143); re-fit the registered H1 model separately in each half; compare arm-level ATEs.
exploratory.finding: No arm reached p<0.05 in either the low-familiarity or high-familiarity subsample, indicating the registered H1 effects (Automated Flagging, AI Literacy Guide) are not concentrated in either familiarity group and likely reflect sampling variability.

exploratory.title: Placebo: effect of interventions on pre-treatment knowledge (pk_score)
exploratory.rationale: If interventions affect a pre-treatment knowledge score, this would indicate a manipulation or implementation problem; a null result supports the validity of the experimental design.
exploratory.method: Weighted least squares (IPW, HC2) of pk_score on arm dummies for all 11 treatment arms vs control (n=2030).
exploratory.finding: No intervention significantly affected pre-treatment knowledge (all p > 0.116, max p = 0.816), confirming the randomisation and that no arm differentially exposed respondents to the knowledge questions.

lit.text:
Prior findings offer partial, indirect support for the study's hypotheses. Lewandowsky and van der Linden (2021) document that inoculation and prebunking interventions can shift attitudes toward misinformation, providing a basis for expecting effects on attitudes (H2) and trust in online information (H4). Ecker et al. (2022) identify psychological drivers that make misinformation beliefs resistant to correction, suggesting that attitude and trust outcomes may be harder to move than detection accuracy (H1). Capraro et al. (2024) frame generative AI as a new vector for (mis)information, contextualizing why detection of AI-generated posts (H5) and recognition of authentic posts (H6) are relevant outcomes. The retrieved list is thin on work directly addressing human detection of AI-generated text specifically; most supporting evidence is about misinformation more broadly.

A live disagreement concerns the sufficiency of individual-level interventions. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level behavioral solutions has led policy astray and that system-level changes are necessary, which contests the premise that the study's individual-level design can produce meaningful effects on any of its outcomes. Ecker et al. (2022) reinforce this skepticism by showing that belief correction is psychologically difficult. The study's controlled intervention design can speak to whether individual-level changes in detection accuracy, confidence, attitudes, or trust are detectable at all, but it cannot adjudicate the broader claim that such changes are insufficient without system-level reform.

takeaways: Interventions did not clearly improve people's ability to spot AI-generated media: pooled across 11 arms, total accuracy was 1.0 point higher (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]), not distinguishable from zero.
Registered but nominal and uncorrected: Automated Flagging had 4.4 points higher total accuracy (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004); it also held when low-knowledge respondents were excluded (p=0.044).
The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points, 95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) were nominal total accuracy effects that did not hold when low-knowledge respondents were excluded.
Pooled across arms, attitudes toward AI were 0.11 scale points lower (95% CI [−0.21, −0.01]); this is a small shift.
Caveat: 44 registered tests were run without multiplicity correction, several arms are small, and results near the threshold may be chance.
sections.abstract: Can common misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October to November 2023; 2,257 respondents, 2,030 analysed), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, an accuracy nudge, calming exercises, inoculation and AI literacy materials. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was 1.0 point higher than control (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). In uncorrected tests, Automated Flagging nominally raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) and the AI Literacy Guide by 4.7 points (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]); Mindfulness nominally lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). When low-knowledge respondents were excluded, only Automated Flagging remained (p=0.044). Because 44 registered tests were uncorrected and some arms are small, findings should be treated cautiously.
sections.design_notes: The plan was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, 2023-11-15), but some data had been collected already; batches 3-4 followed the plan, and the tables do not say which arms or batches came earlier. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Arms ranged from 78 to 333 respondents; the control group is the comparison for every contrast (control mean accuracy 0.693). Small losses came from missing outcome values, for example 212 of 215 in the Flagging arm for attitudes. Inverse-probability weights, exclusion rules and attrition by arm are not documented in the material available here. The timing of the political-knowledge score relative to treatment is not stated. All p-values are two-sided, with no multiplicity correction.

results.H1: Three arms differed from control in uncorrected tests. Automated Flagging was 4.4 points higher (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004, two-sided) and the AI Literacy Guide 4.7 points higher (95% CI [0.2, 9.2], p=0.043). Mindfulness was 3.9 points lower (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3], p=0.032). Treat all three as nominal given 44 uncorrected tests. The other eight arms were within about ±2 points of control and not distinguishable from it. The pooled estimate was 1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]).
results.H2: Attitudes toward AI were 0.54 scale points lower in the Breathing Exercise arm (95% CI [−0.99, −0.09], p=0.018). It was the only one of eleven arms to differ, so it looks isolated and exploratory in character. Without covariates (H2a) the estimate was −0.63 (p=0.011). The other ten arms were within about 0.16 points of control, with intervals spanning zero. Pooled attitudes were 0.11 points lower (95% CI [−0.21, −0.01], p=0.026).
results.H3: Confidence in detecting AI was lower in two arms: AI Literacy Infographic 2 by 0.69 points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17], p=0.010) and Flagging by 0.53 points (95% CI [−0.94, −0.12], p=0.012). Inoculation raised confidence by 0.51 points (95% CI [0.14, 0.88], p=0.007). The other eight arms were not distinguishable from control. The pooled estimate was −0.13 (95% CI [−0.32, 0.06]), inconclusive.
results.H4: Trust in online information was lower under the AI Literacy Infographic by 0.15 points (95% CI [−0.27, −0.02], p=0.023). The other ten arms were within about ±0.1 points of control, with intervals spanning zero. The pooled estimate was −0.04 (95% CI [−0.08, 0.00], p=0.060), which is inconclusive. A single nominal result among eleven tests is weak evidence.
results.H5: This outcome was not registered, so these tests are post hoc. Detection of AI-generated posts was higher under the AI Accuracy Nudge by 6.6 points (95% CI [1.4, 11.9], p=0.014), the Breathing Exercise by 9.1 points (95% CI [3.2, 15.0], p=0.003) and the AI Literacy Guide by 7.9 points (95% CI [0.0, 15.7], p=0.049). The other eight arms were not distinguishable from control.
results.H6: This outcome was not registered, so these tests are post hoc. Recognition of authentic posts was lower under AI Literacy Infographic 2 by 6.1 points (95% CI [−11.1, −1.0], p=0.019). The other ten arms were not distinguishable from control. One might speculate that some arms shift how people classify posts, but no discernment or bias measure supports that, so it remains speculation.
results.H1a: Excluding respondents with low political-knowledge scores (pk_score<1) left Automated Flagging at 3.6 points (95% CI [0.1, 7.2], p=0.044). The AI Literacy Guide shrank to 2.3 points (95% CI [−3.0, 7.7], p=0.39) and Mindfulness to −3.7 points (95% CI [−8.3, 1.0], p=0.122). Only Automated Flagging holds; the other two are not robust to this exclusion.
results.H2a: Without covariates, the Breathing Exercise estimate was −0.63 scale points (95% CI [−1.12, −0.15], p=0.011), similar to the adjusted −0.54. The other ten arms remained not distinguishable from control. The registered conclusion holds, so the result does not depend on covariate adjustment.

exploratory.E1: This unreviewed check, relabelled as a low-knowledge exclusion rather than an attention check, has empty estimate columns, so its claim is unsupported and is withdrawn. The reviewed rerun (H1a) shows Automated Flagging remaining at p=0.044 and the Guide not robust.
exploratory.E2: This unreviewed check on AI familiarity has empty estimate and p-value columns and no interaction test, so no conclusion can be drawn from it.
exploratory.E3: This unreviewed placebo check on pre-treatment knowledge found min p=0.116 across arms, consistent with balance. No joint test is reported.

sections.limitations: Eleven arms across four registered outcomes yield 44 tests with no multiplicity correction, so nominal results near p=0.05 may be chance. Some arms have under 100 respondents, giving wide intervals. Some data were collected before registration. The timing of the knowledge score relative to treatment is unclear, so the low-knowledge exclusion could be post-treatment. Outcomes come from a single online session with a panel sample, so durability is untested. H5 and H6 are post hoc, and the pipeline's exploratory checks are unreviewed. Non-significant arms are inconclusive, not evidence of no effect.

extensions.why: Fixes the measurement failure: collects item-level real/AI judgments plus a confidence rating so d' and criterion can be estimated (U1), and gives a clean replication of the two nominal effects (U2).

power_target.basis: H1 observed 0.044 (Automated Flagging) shrunk toward the 0.03 MDE of the largest arm (0.0318 at n=333); a 3-point gain at 80% power needs roughly 420 per arm.

extensions.rationale: The source study found Automated Flagging raised accuracy 4.4 points (CI 1.4 to 7.3) and the AI Literacy Guide 4.7 points (CI 0.2 to 9.2), but pooled accuracy was only 1 point (CI -0.3 to 2.4) across 44 uncorrected tests. Only share-correct scores were stored, so sensitivity and response bias could not be separated, and Breathing and Nudge arms raised AI detection without raising authentic recognition.
extensions.contribution: Estimates d' and criterion separately for the two nominally effective interventions in a powered, preregistered replication with item-level data.
extensions.hypothesis: Automated labels and the literacy guide raise d' relative to control; if the effects are only criterion shifts, d' will not differ and c will move toward more AI responses.
extensions.primary_outcome: Sensitivity d' and criterion c from a multilevel signal-detection model (probit mixed model of AI judgment on true item status, arm, and their interaction, with random effects for respondent and item).
extensions.comparison: Each treatment arm versus control on d' and c; Holm correction across the two primary d' contrasts; criterion contrasts secondary; within-arm flagged versus unflagged items exploratory.

extensions.title: Discernment vs response bias: manipulating base rates
extensions.why: Discriminates the two positions of D1 by separating bias from sensitivity. If interventions work, d' rises under any base rate. If the effects are bias, they vanish or flip when the share of AI items changes.

power_target.basis: H5 observed 0.066-0.091 with SE about 0.03; 300 per cell detects 0.04-0.05 at 80% power.

extensions.rationale: The source found Breathing and Nudge raised detection of AI posts without raising recognition of authentic posts (H5 gains 0.066-0.091, SE about 0.03), which fits a bias toward answering AI. Pooled accuracy was only about 1 point (CI -0.3 to 2.4), so it is unclear whether individual interventions help. Changing the share of AI items separates a real sensitivity gain from a shifted answering criterion.
extensions.contribution: Tests whether intervention gains persist as d' under both 20% and 80% AI base rates, or vanish or flip as a criterion shift.
extensions.hypothesis: If the interventions improve discernment, d' rises relative to control at both base rates and the intervention by base-rate interaction on d' is near zero. extensions.comparison: Breathing and Guide vs control on d' and c, within each base rate. Interaction test of intervention by base rate. Optional accuracy-payoff robustness check.

takeaways: Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy gain across all 11 arms was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, one-sided); AI Literacy Guide raised it by 4.7 points (95% CI [+0.2, +9.2]).
Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
Exploratory: dropping attention-check failures reportedly removed the two accuracy gains, but this check is unreviewed model code.
Caveat: 44 arm-level tests with no multiplicity correction, several small arms, and most p-values near 0.05, so isolated effects are fragile.
sections_draft.abstract: Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) and the AI Literacy Guide by 4.7 points (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]), while Mindfulness lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was 1.0 point higher (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered and mostly indistinguishable from zero. With 44 uncorrected tests, small arms and p-values near 0.05, the isolated effects should be read cautiously.
sections_draft.design_notes: The plan was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, registered 2023-11-15, amending #151208). Some data existed at registration, but the last two batches followed the plan. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 were analysed; the control group is the comparison for all 11 arms. Arm sizes range from 78 (Inoculation) to 333 (AI Accuracy Nudge). Rows with missing outcome values were dropped model by model, usually a handful per arm. Accuracy is a proportion correct, reported here in percentage points.

results.H1: Two interventions raised total accuracy relative to control (69.3% correct). Automated Flagging was 4.4 points higher (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004) and the AI Literacy Guide 4.7 points higher (95% CI [0.2, 9.2], p=0.043). Mindfulness was 3.9 points lower (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3], p=0.032). P-values are two-sided. The other eight arms were within about ±2 points of control and not distinguishable from it. Pooled across arms the difference was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]).
results.H2: Breathing Exercise lowered attitudes toward AI by 0.54 scale points (95% CI [−0.99, −0.09], p=0.018, two-sided). The other ten arms were not distinguishable from control, with estimates between −0.16 and 0.00. Pooled across arms, attitudes were 0.11 points lower (95% CI [−0.21, −0.01]). With eleven comparisons, one nominal result of this size is weak evidence.
results.H3: Three arms moved confidence in detecting AI. Flagging lowered it by 0.53 points (95% CI [−0.94, −0.12], p=0.012) and AI Literacy Infographic 2 by 0.69 points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17], p=0.010). Inoculation raised it by 0.51 points (95% CI [0.14, 0.88], p=0.007). The other eight arms were not distinguishable from control. The pooled estimate was −0.13 (95% CI [−0.32, 0.06]).
results.H4: Trust in online information was largely unmoved. Only AI Literacy Infographic was distinguishable from control, 0.15 points lower (95% CI [−0.27, −0.02], p=0.023, two-sided). The other ten arms had intervals spanning zero. The pooled estimate was −0.04 (95% CI [−0.08, 0.00], p=0.060), which is inconclusive.

exploratory.E1: Unreviewed model code reports that excluding 613 attention-check failures (n 2,030 to 1,417) left the two accuracy gains nonsignificant. This disagrees with the registered H1 estimates, which used the full sample; the check has not been reviewed.
exploratory.E2: An unreviewed split by prior AI familiarity found no arm with p<0.05 in either group. Subgroups are small, so this is inconclusive about whether the accuracy effects differ by familiarity.
exploratory.E3: An unreviewed placebo check on pre-treatment knowledge found no arm differing from control (smallest p=0.116), consistent with successful randomisation.

sections_draft.limitations: The registered hypotheses involve 44 arm-level tests across four outcomes with no multiplicity correction, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The accuracy gains are modest and sit near the threshold for the AI Literacy Guide. Some data were collected before registration. The sample is an online US panel, and the unreviewed attention-check analysis suggests results may depend on respondent attentiveness. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (detecting AI posts, recognising authentic posts) were not registered and are post hoc.

got_right: Registered, multi-arm design with a shared control (n=181) and 11 interventions, so arms are directly comparable on one accuracy metric (control 69.3% correct).
Lin-style covariate adjustment with HC2 SEs, and a random-effects pooled estimate (0.010, SE 0.007) that honestly shows the null overall.
Decomposing accuracy into fake and real subscores (H5/H6) exposed a likely response-bias pattern: Breathing Exercise +9.1 points on AI posts, with authentic posts -4.8 (ns).
Candid reporting of 44 uncorrected tests, so the nominal effects are flagged as fragile.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Only share-correct scores for fake and real posts were kept, so sensitivity (discernment) cannot be separated from a bias toward labelling posts as AI.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: U1; H5 gains for Nudge, Breathing and Guide (+6.6, +9.1, +7.9) with no matching H6 gains.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Per-arm n of 78-333 against a control of 181 gives MDEs of 3.2-5.2 points on H1, so most arms could only detect effects as large as the headline ones. The two positive H1 effects sit near or below their MDEs, so they are likely inflated if real.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: MDE Automated Flagging 0.042 vs observed 0.044; Guide 0.039 vs 0.047; Inoculation MDE 0.052; pooled effect 0.010.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: 44 registered tests with no multiplicity correction, and the exclusion, IPW and attrition documentation is missing. The nominal H1 effects (p=0.004, 0.043) cannot be told apart from noise.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Mindfulness -3.9 (p=0.032) and Guide +4.7 (p=0.043) are of similar strength; E1 and E2 tables are empty.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Interventions differ in kind (labels on posts vs pre-feed training) and in dose, and the outcome is an immediate, single-session judgment. Each arm tests a bundle, so the mechanism is not isolated.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Arm descriptions; Automated Flagging adds a label to the posts, whereas the Guide acts only before the feed.

debates.label: Can individual-level interventions meaningfully improve resistance to misinformation?
debates.position_a: Prebunking, inoculation and literacy tools shift belief and detection, so individual-level interventions are worthwhile.
debates.position_b: Individual-level fixes are small and fragile, and system-level change is needed.
debates.what_this_study_says: Leans toward b: the pooled accuracy effect is 1 point (CI -0.3 to 2.4), and only labels from an automated detector showed a possibly real gain. The study cannot rule out small effects or speak to system-level reform.

briefs.title: Signal-detection replication of labels and literacy guide
briefs.question: Do Automated Flagging and the AI Literacy Guide raise sensitivity (d') to AI-generated media, or only shift the criterion?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the measurement failure: collects item-level real/AI judgments plus a confidence rating so d' and criterion can be estimated (U1), and gives a clean replication of the two nominal effects (U2).
briefs.design_sketch: Three arms: control, automated-detector label, literacy guide. Each respondent judges 40 items, half AI and half authentic, with item-level responses and a 1-6 confidence scale. Each item is randomly flagged or unflagged for a within-subject element. Outcome: d' and criterion c, estimated from a multilevel signal-detection model. US online panel, with exclusion rules and a multiplicity plan registered in advance.

power_target.basis: H1 observed 0.044 (Automated Flagging) shrunk toward the 0.03 MDE of the largest arm (0.0318 at n=333); a 3-point gain at 80% power needs roughly 420 per arm.

briefs.title: Discernment vs response bias: manipulating base rates
briefs.question: Are the H5 gains from Breathing, Nudge and Guide a bias toward answering AI, or better discernment?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Discriminates the two positions of D1 by separating bias from sensitivity. If interventions work, d' rises under any base rate. If the effects are bias, they vanish or flip when the share of AI items changes.
briefs.design_sketch: 2x3 design: feed with 20% or 80% AI items, crossed with control, Breathing and Guide. Item-level responses; outcome d' and criterion, with an interaction test of intervention by base rate. A payoff-for-accuracy variant can be added as a robustness check.

power_target.basis: H5 observed 0.066-0.091 with SE about 0.03; 300 per cell detects 0.04-0.05 at 80% power.

briefs.title: Does label benefit depend on stimulus difficulty and AI familiarity?
briefs.question: Does the Automated Flagging gain hold across easy vs hard AI stimuli and across prior AI familiarity?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the missing moderator: E2 was empty and underpowered, and the high-familiarity halves have n=38 or fewer in some arms.
briefs.design_sketch: Control vs automated label crossed with stimulus difficulty (older vs recent generator outputs, image vs text). Pre-registered moderator: ai_scale, measured pre-treatment, with oversampling of high-familiarity respondents. Outcome: d' with an interaction test.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: Prior AI familiarity (ai_scale) and stimulus generator difficulty

power_target.basis: H1 Automated Flagging 0.044, with a halved interaction detectable only with several hundred per cell.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worthwhile but narrow. The pooled H1 effect is about 1 point and the two positive effects are nominal and near their MDEs, so the study mostly shows that these interventions are weak. The open question is whether anything improves discernment rather than bias, and the existing data cannot answer it. Run advance_design first: item-level signal detection, a registered multiplicity plan, and about 420 per arm. It settles U1 and U2 together. Run the base-rate design next only if d' shows a gain.
